title: Finite-Particle Quantum Reduction of Thermodynamic Irreversibility
abstract: Thermodynamics is useful because it lets us predict and control complex systems from a few accessible quantities when microscopic reconstruction is impractical. We ask whether this operational reduction can be less costly in a finite quantum system than in a matched classical one. We compare a few-boson Bose--Hubbard chain with its number-conserving classical-field counterpart under the same driving and the same coarse spatial record. The quantum system relaxes more in the observed particle distribution, yet the retained mean energy resolves more of the microscopic structure hidden by that record, leaving less information unusable and smaller entropy generation. We then close the process into a heat-engine cycle whose controls use only the measured mean energy and spatial record, not full state tomography; at matched thermal resources, the smaller entropy generation gives more work and higher efficiency. The advantage fades as the particle number grows toward the classical-field regime.
summary: This work compares the thermodynamic irreversibility costs between a finite quantum Bose-Hubbard chain and its classical counterpart when information is limited to coarse measurements. The authors demonstrate that retaining mean energy alongside the spatial record allows the quantum system to generate less entropy and extract more work. This quantum advantage is robustly confirmed across various numerical tests but vanishes in the classical limit.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether the operational reduction of information (coarse-graining) in a finite quantum system incurs less thermodynamic irreversibility cost compared to its matched classical counterpart.
main_result: The quantum system exhibits smaller entropy generation and higher work output during thermodynamic cycles compared to the classical field, an advantage that diminishes as the particle number approaches the classical limit.
method: The analysis uses information-theoretic tools, comparing entropy generation ($\Sigma$) across different coarse-grained descriptions (spatial record $R$ vs. combined energy and record $(E, R)$) for a heat-engine cycle.
model_or_system: The study compares a finite-particle Bose-Hubbard quantum chain with its number-conserving classical-field counterpart, using matched Hamiltonians for comparison.
key_observables: Entropy generation ($\Sigma_{Q}^{BC}$ vs. $\Sigma_{cl}^{BC}$), work output, and the information gaps ($G_R, A_E, I_{E,R}$).
important_parameters: Particle number ($Q$), interaction strength ($g/J$), and the thermal bath temperature ($T_h$).
main_assumptions: The comparison is restricted to the information contained in the record $(E, R)$, not full state tomography, and the advantage fades as $Q$ increases.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the matched quantum-classical construction, the three relevant states ($ho,  ar{ho}_R,  ar{ho}_{E,R}$), and the quantitative comparison of entropy generation across different protocols and parameter variations.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework by defining information reduction via entropy gaps, applies this to a heat-engine cycle comparison between quantum and classical systems, and then rigorously tests the resulting inequality ($\Sigma_Q < \Sigma_{cl}$) through various numerical and physical robustness checks.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, information-theoretic framework for quantifying the quantum advantage in non-equilibrium thermodynamics, particularly when system size is finite and coarse measurements are necessary.
